parsed.summary: The Lean theorem proves two things. First, for every real C > 0 there are n > 0 and a nonconstant function f : {±1}^n → {±1} (encoded as Bool-valued inputs and ℝ-valued outputs in {−1, 1}) whose signed sum of singleton Fourier coefficients exceeds C·√deg(f). Second, the set of ratios Σ_i|f̂({i})|/√deg(f), taken over Boolean f with deg(f) > 0, is not bounded above. The definitions of the uniform average, the characters, the Fourier coefficients and the real Fourier degree (sup of |S| over nonzero f̂(S), which is 0 for constants) match the paper. I found no material caveat: the junk-value risks (division, empty sup, cardinality zero) are all neutralized by the hypotheses or are harmless.

glossary.plain: uniform expectation E over a finite type
glossary.note: The cube has cardinality 2^n ≥ 1, so the inverse of the cardinality is never junk.

glossary.plain: deg(f) = max{|S| : f̂(S) ≠ 0}, and 0 if there is no such S
glossary.note: An empty sup gives 0, matching 'constants have degree zero'.

glossary.plain: f takes two different values somewhere
∀C>0 ∃n>0 ∃ Boolean nonconstant f on n bits with C√deg f < Σ_i f̂({i})
the set {Σ_i|f̂({i})|/√deg f : n>0, f Boolean, deg f > 0}
glossary.standard_concept: the set whose supremum appears in Theorem 1.1

lean_claims.plain: (∀C>0 ∃n>0 ∃f:{±1}^n→{±1} nonconstant with Σ_i f̂({i}) > C√deg(f)) ∧ the set {Σ_i|f̂({i})|/√deg(f) : n≥1, f Boolean, deg(f)>0} is not bounded above in ℝ.

paper_claims.plain: For every C>0 there are n≥1 and a nonconstant Boolean f with Σ_i f̂({i}) > C√deg(f). Consequently, the supremum over n≥1 and Boolean f with deg(f)>0 of Σ|f̂({i})|/√deg(f) is ∞.

coverage.why: Both clauses are formalized faithfully. 'Not bounded above' is the real-valued rendering of sup = ∞.

lint_verdicts.why: The average is only applied over Cube (Fin n), which has cardinality 2^n ≥ 1.
The empty-sup default of 0 matches the paper's convention that constants have degree zero, and the second clause separately requires deg > 0.
The hypothesis 0 < fourierDegree f makes √deg strictly positive, so the division is never by zero.
